utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Tom Hannis, Belinda Pidwell, and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. For the Stanisic Defence team, Slobodan Cvijetic, Ms. Tatjana Savic, and Ms. Deirdre Montgomery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Igor Pantelic, and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. We have been alerted that there are some preliminary matters before the witness resumes his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Just one very short item, Your Honours. We don't have any cross-examination estimates for two of the witnesses that are scheduled to testify later this week, and I'm wondering if I could be provided with them during the course of the day. They're the first two of the new witnesses which have been added as a result of the adjudicated facts decision, and we -- they're viva voce. So it would be appreciated if we could have the estimates to know exactly what to say to the witness when they arrive and to liaise with VWS about their length of stay. And I'm also wondering, we have -- the next witness is ST-098, Ewa Tabeau. The current estimate I have for her provided by the Defence quite a while ago was four hours each for cross-examination, and I'm just wondering if that has been revised in any way during the course of the preparation so we can schedule the balance of the witnesses accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So -- yes, Mr. Krgovic, you're in a position to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as for these two witnesses testifying about adjudicated facts, the Defence team has a dilemma. Specifically the witness scheduled to witness [as interpreted] this week about an adjudicated fact which is very short, only two and a half hours are scheduled. If the OTP, in accordance with the Chamber's ruling, wants only to show that adjudicated facts and establish the circumstances for which the witness was called, we may not have more than 25 minutes of cross-examination. But if the OTP use two and a half hours and extend their examination-in-chief, we will apply for additional time to cross-examine the witness. That's why we think that the OTP should shorten the time allotted to them for the examination-in-chief and focus only on the adjudicated facts, because that's how we understand the ruling of the Bench, namely, that both the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination will deal only with the adjudicated facts. Given that, we don't expect to have many questions for the witnesses that will come to testify about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on behalf of the Stanisic Defence, I would like to say something about the witnesses called to testify about adjudicated facts. My estimate is one session for each of them, and that is a generous estimate. We may actually need less. As for the expert witness, we applied for four hours, as Ms. Pidwell said, but that is also a very generous estimate. We expect to use much less, indeed. But it certainly depends on what we are going to hear in the courtroom. But, anyway, we will certainly not exceed four hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Pidwell, now you know, or don't know, where you stand. We will see.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I guess that's the best -- that's as good as it's going to get at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It would perhaps be useful if we can have confirmation from Ms. Pidwell that the scope of the examination-in-chief will only be the adjudicated fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we're very aware of the terms of your ruling, and our interpretation is that it's the adjudicated fact plus contextual evidence to provide the context of the -- of the fact. So we're aware of that, and that's the basis on which we're proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, maybe we should make good use of the time before the witness comes in. While examining one of the previous protected witnesses, and I'm referring to ST-215, the Trial Chamber admitted a document of the Defence. The page reference is 14.962 of the transcript, and it was given the exhibit number 1D384, MFI. This mark for identification was applied because on that day we couldn't provide an English translation. In the meantime, however, I have been informed that the translation is ready, so my motion would be to remove the MFI tag.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So ordered. I'm trying to avoid the use of the term de-MFI, which is the jargon of the Tribunal. It seems to be such an ugly concept, but we all know what we mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: While we're on this topic, perhaps I can clarify one matter as well. Your Honours will recall yesterday the issue of the -- exhibiting the newspaper article of the 17th of July, and it was admitted on the basis of the date only and not the contents. As it turns out, that article has previously been tendered through a previous witness who was able to speak to the contents of the article. It was -- it's actually P1378. And accordingly, in order to avoid any complications in the future in regards to this article, I seek leave to withdraw the exhibit that was tendered yesterday on that limited basis, because it's already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So ordered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can the Registrar indicate the number we had put yesterday? Did you check ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, good morning to you, sir. I trust that you are recovered from --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- from yesterday and that you are able to go on. I would remind you that you're still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Miskovic.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, yesterday we broke off when we discussed the talks with representatives of Kozarac. I asked you about the level of these talks and partly about the topics discussed and also about the participants.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You said to me then that the talks were held at the local level.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And that nobody outside of Prijedor took part.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody but us. That was our organisation and it was our concept, so nobody had any influence on that, nor any suggestions. Whether anybody subsequently applied the same rules, I don't know. But it was our idea. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zupljanin did not take part in these talks about Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't. As I said so. Only on one occasion when we were in Omarska, and I tried to reach him once after talking to a Radovan Karadzic. A man whom I knew from before the war as a colleague, I met him only once, but we had no connections whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you took a personal interest in resolving the issue of Kozarac. If -- you would know if Mr. Zupljanin had taken part?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I certainly would have. Not only about him but anybody else too. That's quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to read Nusret Sivac's book: "How Large is the Carsija of Prijedor"?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't read it, but I've heard of it. But I have no need to read of these things because I was directly involved. I heard that my name is mentioned there too, probably because I was a protagonist of the events. I hope I'm not being mentioned in a negative context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you may want to read it after all.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. If I do reading something, I'll read something more serious. I met Sivac later, two years ago, actually. He was a communications man with the police. He worked with us, and he also was a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Krgovic, just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think we should clarify the transcript where the witness gives evidence about the -- about Kozarac and the question whether Mr. Zupljanin knew about it. And he said: "Nobody but us. That was our organisation and it was our concept, so nobody had any influence on that, nor any suggestions." I skip one -- one line. "... it was our idea. I apologise." And the "I apologise" could be misunderstood. The witness just coughed and said "I apologise" because he coughed, and nothing else. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, while we are on this particular issue of whether or not Mr. Zupljanin was involved in the planning of the events in Kozarac, could I ask the witness whether Mr. Zupljanin was subsequently informed of these events? Because I think you told us yesterday that the local police was involved in that operation, so I assume that at some point Mr. Zupljanin would have been informed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said it was our idea, and I was saying so talking both to the Prosecution and to the Defence, it means that we organised all activities independently with all structures from the Prijedor municipality to prevent confrontation there. And that was the context of all the activities. As for the activities in Kozarac, talks were held, and I -- and the context of these talks was explained yesterday, about those insignia, et cetera, the functioning of the police, the police station in Ljubija and in Kozarac after the takeover of power and everything. As for the activities and the operation, the shelling of Kozarac, that is, the military operation, it was a military operation. The military did it. So that was along the military lines of command. Whether the police took part in it, and, if so, to what extent, I don't know, because it was a military operation. The military had all the equipment used there, and they commanded everything and all that. And that's how it was in other parts of Prijedor too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I owe an explanation to Judge Harhoff. I asked this line of questions because this witness whose book I mentioned writes that Mr. Zupljanin was involved in the talks in Kozarac, and that is the reason why --

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has said he hasn't read the book. And I'm wondering if it's appropriate for him to be listening to this line of explanation from my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I hear your objection, Ms. Pidwell, but I'm not sure that any harm is done inasmuch as when he said he hadn't read the book, he said he was involved in the incident, so I don't see a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have just finished with that line of questioning. I just want to explain why I asked the witness about that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, speaking about these meetings and the appearance of certain people in Prijedor, let me ask you, you have certainly heard of General Subotic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I knew Goran Subotic. In Banja Luka, at meetings, he held some sort of position at the top. I don't know which position. I know that later on he was in charge of pensions and medals and other things, but I wasn't with the party anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In August 1992, and in September, did you hear that Mr. Subotic came to Prijedor, together with Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only know that General Talic once came. I remember that. I was leaving the Municipal Assembly building and he was just parking his vehicle and coming out of it, and he had brought military camouflage uniforms, summer uniforms. I remember that, and I got one. And that's why I can be seen in many pictures and on the radio in that period. And General Talic came once. I don't know whether he ever came again though. I was invited to come to the corps command because I often reacted to the looting and other crimes such as smuggling and so on, so people from the region would be summoned to come to the corps command to find out what's going on. And then the issue was raised how it's possible that the trucks can go through all the 50 check-points from our territory to Serbia, whereas I cannot even take a pin through those check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday the Prosecutor showed you a video. That's not the video showing the occasion when you visited, and you didn't see the people that were with you then?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember which video you're referring to. But I was there only once, and we clarified that with the Prosecution and the Defence. Just once. At Trnopolje and Keraterm, those are places I never went to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When the delegation from Banja Luka arrived, the -- the visit of that delegation in -- to Omarska on the upper floor was all recorded. You saw it; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a camera recording was made. And I wonder how come that footage isn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Part of my question is missing. You saw it later on television of RS; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And it was in the local newspaper, the "Kozarski Vjesnik."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you were at that meeting on the upper floor in Omarska, as far as I understood your testimony, two topics were discussed, to your memory. The functioning of the investigation centre and the examination techniques; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember all the details because it was a long time ago. But the briefing was mostly about the conditions in the facility and the activities that had been taken. And also ongoing activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And when the situation in the facility was discussed, none of the participants from the delegation or from there said that the conditions were bad and nobody complained about anything. Everybody said basically that it was consistent with the given circumstances and conditions?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the circumstances under which the facilities operated at the time. And those who managed the facilities said all the best, that everything was working well, that everything necessary has been supplied, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And it was your understanding then, in Prijedor, was that all these investigation centres, as they were called, had been established so that people who were suspected of involvement in armed operations needed to be screened to find out who was responsible?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I understood, that the professional police was inquiring into the involvement of every individual so that charges be brought against those who are found to be responsible and the others released. That's how -- how the normal police procedure would run. Now, if that procedure was really observed, I don't know. I didn't know many things. You -- you told me that there were no criminal complaints filed, and that surprises me. I didn't know at the time that not a single criminal complaint has been filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one correction to the transcript. The witness said: You told me that there were criminal complaints filed, and I didn't know at the time that criminal complaints were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You said a few days ago that criminal complaints were filed against individuals with the District Prosecutor's Office, and I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I'm not exactly clear about what we are talking about here. I don't know if Mr. Krgovic can clarify. Criminal complaints filed by whom against whom? That seems to be an open question. But, Mr. Miskovic, are you able to give an estimation as to the number of persons detained at Omarska when you went to visit the place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the criminal complaints, that relates to criminal complaints against persons who had been brought to the investigation centre in Omarska, and the criminal complaints are normally filed by the police officers who interrogated these people, active-duty and reserve policemen. Now, as for the estimate, it is very difficult for me to estimate - I'm not good at that - but let's say, roughly, from what I've seen, there could have been 150 to 200 people. I don't know. It would be really silly of me to give any definite number, but that would be a rough figure. There was a fence between us and there was a line of people on the other side of the fence. They were lined up. But I'm really surprised that there is no video footage. Everything was recorded, including the meeting in the conference hall, and I thought you had that material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: To your recollection, did the staff at the Omarska camp provide you with any information about how many people were detained there at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. You told us yesterday that you were given an introductory speech by the camp command. And so I wonder if, during that speech, information was provided to you as to the number of persons detained at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now in hindsight, 20 years later, I cannot remember that discussion. But as soon as the delegation arrived, the host - in this case, the warden of the investigation centre - gave a briefing about the centre, the number of people, the activities undertaken, and the measures taken against individuals. I can only suppose that that's what we had come for. It was not to take pictures. It was an official delegation visiting the centre. And on behalf of the centre, their manager made a report, and that's what he should have covered. He could not have talked about anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one follow-up question, Mr. Miskovic. Did the delegation tour the facility, the camp? Did they go around, see what happened? Or did they only go upstairs to the meeting room and -- and then left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was literally the way you put it at the end. We got out of the car, we climbed the stairs, got into the conference room, received the information that I just mentioned. After that, we got back into the car and left. I don't know where the others went, but I went to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And -- and you -- when you say you left, that applies for you as well as for the Banja Luka delegation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody -- nobody toured any other buildings. We only got upstairs, went into that room, went down the same stairs, and left. I don't know if anyone came to visit later, but that visit passed exactly as I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, just one more thing regarding this visit. You told us about your knowledge at the time, that it was an investigation centre, that people suspected of involvement --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People assumed to have been involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, people thought to have been involved in the armed insurgency were being screened, interrogated, to see whether evidence existed and in relation to whom?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I understood, and that's why in all my evidence I said that in my eyes it was an investigation centre because these people were interrogated by professionals who were trained. Now to what extent triage was made, whether it was made, I don't know. But professionally speaking, that's the way it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And that's what the delegation from -- from Prijedor was told, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you I can't remember after 20 years. But I suppose, judging from the context, that it was the only thing that could have been talked about, because the director of the centre could have only made a briefing about that; the situation in Omarska and the problems. Now, what details he covered, I don't remember anymore. If you had asked me earlier, I would have recalled it better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Regarding the condition of the buildings in Omarska that you toured, those were newly built facilities; they were in good condition at the time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was commander of the section in Omarska when preparations were made for extraction of the ore. I worked on the expropriation of land and similar matters, so I know exactly who the contractor was. It was Hidrogradnja company from Sarajevo. I was on good terms with that business because of my role. And those buildings were built at that time. They were fresh, newly built, including all the appointment and equipment for that sort of facility. At the time, it was a modern building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, I will show you now a document --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And you can see that on the footage, that those were solid, good buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P602 is the document we need displayed to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, this is a report of the commission that was set up in August 1998.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I meant -- sorry, I meant 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown the last page. In Serbian, it's page 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is a report made by a commission. Do you know any of the people named here?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Vaso Skondric. We studied together. Vojin Bera, I know him. Ranko Mijic, I know him. And Jugoslav Rodic I also know; he worked in the security service. I know all of them. They are all from the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Miskovic, that these people came to Prijedor more than once and that they toured the investigation centre?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. They did not approach me. They did not contact me. I'm seeing this document for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown the fourth page of this document in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be enlarged a bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On page 4 the condition of the facility in Omarska is described. I'll read out to you just one passage that begins with the words: "Since this was a relatively new facility which had all the necessary living and residential conditions for a larger number of persons (offices, halls, toilets and washrooms, kitchen and dining-room, constant supply of drinking water, a large number of showers, constant supply of electricity, a generator, and so on), no alterations were made to the building, but the existing premises were used instead for the accommodation of and work with the prisoners." Is this a correct description of that facility, to the best of your knowledge? Did you really see that? Does that hall exist? And all the other conditions stated here?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, I just said a moment ago I was a section commander in Omarska when this was built, and preparations were made for the extraction of the ore. But I never went inside the building, and I don't know the layout inside, what the conditions were. But I suppose that these buildings were later adapted for the accommodation of workers who were probably using washrooms and bathrooms, et cetera. That probably existed, although I didn't see it. All I saw during the visit was the conference hall where I went with the delegation. That's all I saw of the inside. And that building was made for that purpose, so it probably had all this. I just didn't go in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, while we're talking about the conditions, in the summer before the corridor was opened, in the summer of 1992, what was the situation inside the city of Prijedor itself, regarding electricity, water supply? What were the prevailing conditions for the other citizens?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, electricity and water supply were a problem. We had occasional supply and occasional blackouts. And I tried, in Celpak at the time, to reactivate a power plant that was not in use at the time. And I remembered one man who had been abroad and then came back to Prijedor, and I asked him if there was any way of reactivating that power plant, and he said he to go and see for himself. He went to see the manager. He said it was impossible to reactivate it. And my next idea was to try mini power plants on the Sana River, that he should analyse that possibility as an expert. So we were looking for alternative sources of energy in the territory. But nothing came out of that, and the situation was with -- was characterised by shortages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the water supply depended on a pump so that when the pump was not working, due to lack of electricity, there was no water either.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the same today. There are large wells near the River Sana, water is pumped out of the river, and currently we got a grant from the Swiss government to finance a project of providing potable water to the city of Prijedor in a different way. Omarska, for instance, always had problems with water. And after all the visits and talks where I participated, we tried to improve the water supply, but it never happened. And now, finally, thanks to this Swiss project, it will have a reliable water supply, finally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the situation for the citizens of Prijedor was not really good until the corridor was broken. There was no or very little food and other needs?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, with the food, yes, at first we had enough supplies. But once they were exhausted, then it was a problem. The water-related problems were -- I felt them myself. My family had to go get water in buckets and then fill the washing machine. I made a well, which is something we're still using, but that's not drinking water, of course. And from the waterworks system, we used that water for drinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you something in relation to the question put by Judge Harhoff. You said that at the time you didn't know about criminal complaints or reports being submitted. Now I will show you a document and then ask you whether you know about the incident that's described in this complaint or report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 2D03-1189. Can we please enlarge it? It's a rather poor copy.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the incidents?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Asim Mujic; Alagic; Devljak; Mithad Kadiric; Murir Kadiric; Samir Cehic; Edin Celic; Bahrija Mulalic; Bajro Borovac; Ferid Crljenkovic; Latif Karagic; Besim Memic; Ermin Dedic; Suad Mrkalj; Mirsad Kadiric, Kina; Sakib Ejupovic; Jasmin Alisic, aka Jama; Hajrudin Ganic, aka Gane; Ibro Grozdanic, aka Geolog; and Sakib Ejupovic, all from Prijedor, are on the run because of a suspicion that all the persons listed under item 3 committed a criminal act of armed rebellion under article 80; yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned that you negotiated with one of the Kadirics in Kozarac. Is any of them here listed?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was Fikret Kadiric who was a police station commander, and he's not here on the list. He was not accused of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please take a look at the last page of the document and tell me whether you can recognise the signature block.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's Radmilo Zeljaja. That's his signature. So this was submitted by the military police. I don't know about this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the army also carried out some investigations and proceedings?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did say that we had civilian and military police and each of the institutions carried out their part of the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 2 of this document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While that page is loading, Mr. Krgovic, I alert you that you have nine minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm completing my cross-examination. This is the last topic. I'll finish within my time allotted to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, do you see this segment where it is mentioned -- and start reading from the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Before the attack on Prijedor..." Is that the part?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That this involves a criminal report against people who attacked Prijedor, which then caused the avalanche of incidents and consequences.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see from the report that it's from that time-period, that the persons mentioned there are the persons who were involved. I knew only one name. I didn't know who was else with him. I knew about all that even before there were attempts through Mr. Sadikovic to get in touch with him and because we knew each other from before the war and tried to sort things out. And I did mention that I went to the barracks and -- to talk to him after the attack, but I don't know whether he felt ashamed; did he feel bad that he didn't take my advice that I sent through him through Dr. Sadikovic. He just left. And so this is about the relevant period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then further in the text, we see that groups that took part in the attack, they are described. Do you know that they came from across -- from the other side of the Sana River?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. A colleague of mine, she lives in one of the flats, in one of the three buildings where you had people from different ethnic groups, and she told me that she had recognised a colleague of hers who was limping, and she saw him crawling next to the building. I only heard it from her. I didn't see it myself. She also told me his name, but that I forgot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know whether I have provided you with sufficient grounds for this, but I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honours. This witness said that he didn't -- wasn't aware of any criminal reports that had been filed in Prijedor, whether civilian or military, and even though he can talk a little bit, very generally, about the -- the contents of the -- purported contents of this document, he can't speak to the truth of it, and he can't speak to the authenticity of it. And it's -- I'm anticipating it's being tendered to prove that criminal reports were, in fact, filed. And he can't give any evidence on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: My question to Mr. Krgovic is -- on his application to tender the document, is to what end?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, precisely because during my examination of the witness, and also during the examination-in-chief, he said that he didn't know about any criminal reports but that he found it strange. And I wanted to illustrate that there were such complaints and that for the purpose were the investigations carried out in investigation centres and so on. But if the Trial Chamber is of the opinion that it is sufficient -- that there isn't a sufficient nexus established, then we can maybe MFI the document and then introduce it through another witness. But I do believe that document is relevant because it demonstrates the cause of all the later incidents, what the witness talked about, the attack, and then disarmament of the military -- of -- of the Muslim paramilitary formations. So this is the purpose of this document. There are two reasons, rather. The first one that I mentioned is that I tried to establish a link with statement by this witness that there were criminal reports; and, secondly, all the facts, attack on Prijedor, the reasons for the later conflict. All that can be seen from this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, the Chamber is wondering if this criminal report is made against anyone who was detained at Omarska, and, indeed, whether the criminal report comes out of the interrogations that were carried out at Omarska. Is there any evidence of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm afraid we will have to then wait for a witness who will come who will talk about this very topic. It is a man who was a member of this mixed team consisting of public and military security services, and he will be able to speak about that. I tried to avoid putting this question to this witness and keep only discussing the adjudicated facts, but I thought maybe because the witness is familiar with the events and because he could recognise the signature of Mr. Zeljaja, that it would be better to use him to introduce this document, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So we will -- thank you. So we will wait. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question, Mr. Miskovic, for the end. You told us about your - how shall I put it? - disagreements with the leadership in Prijedor and with your disapproval of what was going on in Prijedor. You told us that you had problems in your attempts to replace the top echelons of Prijedor authorities.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We even had Municipal Assembly sessions in order to achieve this. I told you, or I told the Prosecutor, that even the military would come to the assemblies carrying rifles headed by their commander, and that was, in a way, pressure exerted against us. Their intention was to make sure that these people would not replaced, but in the end we succeeded. I think I described this to you during my testimony. I think it was while I was answering to the Prosecutor's Office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then you said that the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor managed to replace Simo Drljaca through assistance of Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We initiated that, and he did arrive. He used his authority and assisted us to have Simo Drljaca replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Because he had support both by the local military, the political structures such as Stakic and the others, and it was very difficult to have him replaced.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not the politics. The political structures were for his replacement. But he did have the government structures and the military behind him. I'm talking only about the leadership segment. There was coordination and cooperation between them. And that's why things went the way they went.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the official position of the party of the SDS, of the Executive Board, yourself, was that you did not stand behind Simo Drljaca or the municipal authorities; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we wanted to replace the leadership. I explained why. It took us a while achieve it. The president of the Executive Board, we managed to replace him without too many problems. However, the last one that we had replaced was Mr. Drljaca, who was the chief of MUP. And as I explained, it was only through the assistance of Mr. Krajisnik that we succeeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Miskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Miskovic.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: My name is Slobodan Cvijetic, and I represent Mr. Stanisic. Mr. Krgovic exhausted most of the questions relevant for you. We have an agreement whereby we try and focus our questions in this way, so my cross-examination will consist of only making a few clarifications in relation to your testimony so far. Yesterday you were asked by Madam Pidwell -- or, rather, after she put a question to you, you asked whether you would be allowed to portray the genesis of the events which was something that reflected your fears of something like that happening again --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And fears of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: -- and the steps you took to achieve that. And then in answering to my colleague Mr. Krgovic, you provided a further explanation of all that. However -- we've been monitoring the transcript. And I know you're aware of the way you speak, and because of that, two crucial things failed to make the transcript. We'll deal with those, and then we'll drop that subject. You will agree with me that the area of the municipality of Prijedor and Kozara was an area where, in the course of the Second World War, the largest genocide against Serbian People was committed anywhere in former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot define it precisely like that. First of all, I don't hail from Prijedor; I hail from Kljuc. But, yes, I went to school there since 1959. We have a house there, and we've been living there ever since. However, the historical facts that we studied about in school and the documents that were being shown then, various visits to Jasenovac's memorial area, then stories by people from Kozara region about their memories. All that comprises my knowledge of the so-called Kozara epos. We also had to study Stojanka Majka Knezopoljka's poem by Skender Kulenovic, and then --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last sentence in his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After 18 years only -- only after 18 years the first soldier from Knezopolje could join the army, because there were no one of the right age. But there were two modes of suffering of people from Kozara: One was in the -- one of the groups were those who were part of the 1st Partisan Brigade who were fighting elsewhere; and then also there was another group who remained in the Kozara region and who were taken by Ustashas to Jasenovac camp, whereas children were taken to camp for children in Jastrebarsko. At that time, in Yugoslavia, all the citizens of Yugoslavia had an opportunity to learn about one such story. It was an actress, Frajt - I forget her first name - but after 25 years only she learned of her identity. It was a family from Bosanska Gradiska. She went there to meet the survivors, I think it was an uncle of hers, but she was very grateful to the Frajt family that gave everything necessary to have a normal life. But she is an illustration of how the children had suffered, children who had ended up in the Jastrebarsko camp. Some of them were killed and some were given to families that couldn't have children. So that's the tragedy that remained in the memories of the people from the Kozara region. With new generations, this seemed to have been forgotten. There were new generations there that forgot about all that, but then they found themselves again in a situation, a similar situation, in 1991. Just a moment. For these reasons, I pointed this out to Mirza Mujavic [phoen]. I warned him: Let's not do that. You know what happened in the area. Let us not stir up old fires. He went to secondary school with me and by chance his father and my father did their military service in Varazdin. Life is funny. So it was my moral obligation to warn him about that. It was the same with Fikret Kadiric. I also tried with him. If you read the documents, will you see that I contacted everybody and warned them of this, not to take these things lightly and think that some things can be done without consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that we have now established the historical link with the events that ensued. We don't have to repeat that anymore. I believe it's sufficiently clear now. Let me ask you something else now. The way I understood Variant B, or the way you explained it to us, in essence, it was the establishment of Serb authorities and Serb municipalities in area where the Serbs were the majority population. Or, in other words, the establishment of Serb municipalities by peaceful, political means, which means by establishing a municipality, or Municipal Assembly, and all other bodies that would function in that part of a particular municipality where the Serbs were the majority population. Have I correctly understood the essence of the implementation of that variant in the Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's partly correct. It's a fact that Variant B, in Prijedor municipality, envisaged the establishment of authorities and a Serb municipality. I said as much answering the Prosecutor's question. However, the Serb municipality was never established in Prijedor because of subsequent events. However, representatives of the authorities were appointed, and there are documents from the meetings that were mentioned. Kuruzovic was at the head of the TO; Simo was at the head of the police; Stakic was supposed to take the position of Assembly president, because in the existing authorities he was deputy; and Simo Kovacevic was supposed to become president of the Executive Committee. But all that was only on paper. The document reads: In case of danger for the Serbian People, take action to prevent that from happening. And that was the purpose of all our activities. So only if the Serb people should be in danger. Only in that case, these structures would be activated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now I must be clear. When -- when I said "where the Serbs are the majority population," I meant the local communes and that part of the municipality where the Serbs were the majority population; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was supposed to be like that, but it was never implemented. And I explained as much. It wasn't done so as not to irritate the other side. And then check-points were set up; I explained all that in detail. And all that was successful. There were no incidents. I explained that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That's why I asked you to explain the genesis of the attempt to divide the area. So it was done pursuant to an agreement with the Muslim side, and you went about it until that telefax arrived. So the talks were successful until that moment, and then things were -- started going wrong.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The talks were not about the division but about preventing confrontation, that all of us, in our structure, should keep a lid on those who were more extreme in their views. On the Serb side is -- some White Eagles appeared, but we immediately locked them up. Everybody who tried to stick out and do anything out of the ordinary was immediately neutralized.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now, if you take into consideration the information received from the -- from military security about the preparations of the Muslims for armed conflict and if you consider the undisputed fact that the municipality of Prijedor was attacked - and it was a well-organised military attack by the Muslim forces - you will agree with me when I conclude that taking over power in Prijedor municipality would have some -- been something the Muslims had done, unless the Serbs had been faster. Do you agree with me that there was a real jeopardy of that happening?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The events there, such as shirking some solutions, avoiding them, could give rise to suspicion that they had afterthoughts, a hidden agenda. But I was in no position to know about that. The first information I received about the organisation of armed units was received from Slavko Ecimovic. And through Dr. Esad Sadikovic, I tried to find out whether he knew what that was leading to. And I was surprised that such a person was at the head of all that and that he's willing to engage in such activities. I've already explained what -- what I mean. I have no need to repeat. However, the attack on Prijedor one month after the takeover of power, in that attack they came up to 50 or 70 metres from the MUP or the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. That alone speaks for itself. This was a well-organised and well-targeted military operation. But their unrefutable -- there is unrefutable evidence that they launched this massive attack. I don't know, however, how many people they have, but the military structures certainly do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm done dealing with this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Honour, I believe it's time for the break anyway, so I will move on to another topic after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We would resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let us continue. I noticed that you stated to Ms. Pidwell that the JNA played a role in all the events in Prijedor. I understood you to say that you said that, at that time, you involved the JNA in the talks as the only legal and official armed force on which you could rely as a guarantor of an agreement.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since all units were subordinate to the command of the JNA, and that's been shown in the evidence led by the Prosecution, Commander Arsic and his deputy were involved in the talks, and they were the only armed force. You may remember a document showing that the JNA was unwilling to protect -- in case the JNA was unwilling to protect the Serb people in the area, then we would call upon all Serbs who were in the ranks of the JNA and the police to leave their units, to establish an army and a police to protect the people in the area. But that has already been elaborated during the direct examination. The subsequent events show that they, indeed, became active, and all units were under their command and control. There was a unified command. And there were no -- no others out there who acted on their own. All units were under the command of the army, the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In accordance with the principle of unified command in combat activities, that is, indeed, so. There is only one command at the top of the pyramid; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All units were subordinate to the JNA command in Prijedor, and the commander was Colonel Arsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us clarify the wartime police stations which you spoke about. The information about the wartime police stations and their establishment is something I found in military rules and regulations. Please explain to me this process of establishing such wartime police stations and the drafting of men to serve there. Is that done by the military body in charge?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Yugoslavia, until the war broke out in 1991, the organisation was such that there was the military department, as we called it, which assigned a wartime assignment to everybody so that everybody knew where they belonged, what their position was, where they should report in case of war or imminent threat of war. And the same applied to the police. According to my wartime assignment, I was commander of the reserve police station, Prijedor 2; I explained that already. And that was in force since the early 1970s. There was also training done, because people were assigned to those positions who, in peacetime, did other jobs. But when there was imminent threat of war, they were reassigned to carry out other jobs and take other positions and be ready to do that at any given moment. That is the concept of reserve forces of both the military and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 13 should read "other jobs," rather than "over jobs." That's what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: When I asked you this question, I had in mind the answers you provided to the Prosecutor but also what your statement given to the Tribunal reads. Your position of command of a wartime police station and the personnel other -- personnel assigned to you was actually your wartime assignment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Our wartime assignment, that was given to us by the military department. That's what we called the body that took care of the wartime assignments of able-bodied men, of the able-bodied population.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So let us be precise. That is your wartime assignment, your military assignments, that you get from the military body in charge?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was called the Department of All People's Defence. That was its name. And there was a hierarchical structure in place from the Federation, through the republics, down to the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I will finish with this topic. I was mistaken in believing that it can be found in the evidence of the Prosecution, but now I see that you applied for some sort of certificate. And it says that at the time when you were commander of the wartime police station --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: -- it is entered into your military ID as participation in a war; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will not search for this document because I have a hard time finding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us show the witness another document, Your Honours, 1D00-0924.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, I hope you can read it. Or do you want us to enlarge it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Read it to yourself and then I'll ask you about it.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: As you can see, this is a conclusion of the Crisis Staff dated 6 June 1992. The blockade remains in force. Obviously it was imposed earlier.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And the procedure is outlined for leaving Prijedor municipality. Do you remember the conclusion?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I didn't know about it earlier. Now, having read the conclusion, I can see that it existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. You don't know the document. But do you know about the blockade and the limitation of movement?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I explained the circumstances. There was also a curfew.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So my question is, so this blockade and the limitation of movement and the curfew applied to all citizens, irrespective of their ethnicity; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Even to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Even leaving the Prijedor municipality without a permit wasn't possible, even for you. So if you wanted to go to Banja Luka, you had to apply for a permit; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I needed a permit to leave Prijedor. Or if I wanted to go to Serbia, also I needed a special permit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, it's not entirely clear to me why this blockade was upheld. Judging from the dates of the Crisis Staff's conclusion, this happened just shortly after the attack on Prijedor by the BiH army. So what would the purpose be of preventing people from leaving the town? Mr. Miskovic, can you help us out here?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way I see it is that control was imposed over movements of citizens in order to know who was leaving the town and who was coming in. That's my assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Indeed, that is what we can read from the Crisis Staff's conclusion. But my question is: Immediately after the town had been subject of an attack, presumably in the attempt to take over the control of Prijedor, why would you prevent people from leaving -- I mean, if I, as a normal citizen, had been living in Prijedor at the time, the only thing I would have had in mind would be to -- to get out of there as soon as possible before the next attack would come.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you say is absolutely correct. But there was a blockade in all areas. Just on the way to Serbia, there were 50 check-points you had to pass through. Everyone had to be physically checked and his papers had to be inspected. Some Muslims took other people's documents and travelled to Serbia that way, if they had errands or business there, and then they would return in the same way. Many went to Belgrade, and I would run into them in Belgrade. They were waiting for all this to blow over, in order to return, again, with other people's identity papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The last thing I want to show you -- in fact, a video was shown to you, and I think it was stopped showing a picture of Omarska camp, and I think you recognised it. I have a much better quality photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution won't mind that I didn't announce it because it's just a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But it would be a good thing for you to look at it and to tell us, on your visit to Omarska, where you went.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give you the number: ERN R093-1252.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, I think this is a very good image, a very good quality photograph.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if we could give this electronic pen to Mr. Miskovic for him to show us where he entered and which part of the camp the delegation actually visited.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see where the stairs are, on which building. I suppose it's this one here, judging by the position of the people who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Put a circle around the building where you actually went inside.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose it's this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And put number 1.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. That is, then, the building into which you had gone.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. But there were stairs on the side.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you draw from which direction you came?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how the car drove in. But the car stopped just outside the building, we went straight inside, up the stairs ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I know that I did not announce this document, but it's a photograph that would complement the testimony of this witness. He had told us a lot about this visit, and he has just explained about where exactly he went. And I would like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, I wonder if we could have the witness also indicate just where he was able to observe the line of the prisoners. I think the prisoner -- the witness said that he saw a line of some 150 to 180 prisoners lined up somewhere. Mr. Miskovic, could you indicate on the photo where that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this is the photograph of the facility which we visited - but I'm not sure it is - then the citizens were standing here, in this area, outside. And as we were climbing up the stairs, we saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Could you put number 2 there.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And if this was this building here, then they would have been lined up here. 3 and 4. I can't see, because this is an aerial photograph. It looks like a map on this image. I don't see any elements that I could use to determine in which part we went in. I don't see even the gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if the Trial Chamber is satisfied with your answer and if this clarifies the position enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked. There's something I'm not clear about. Did -- Mr. Miskovic, did I understand your answer to Judge Harhoff's question to be, in effect, that the building that you had originally marked as 1, that it is either that or the building that you marked as 3? Is that the effect of your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just said it. I'm not sure which building it was. If it's building number 1, then the people were lined up as I marked with 2. If it was the building number 3, then the people were lined up as shown in 4. Because I can't see those stairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... okay. Well, bearing in mind that you can't see the stairs, are you able to say, nevertheless -- well, I suppose I should ask, as a preliminary question, whether the room into which you entered had been those which overlooked a portion of the yard. Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember. That room did not overlook this part of the yard where the prisoners were standing. It overlooked the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you. In which -- Thank you. In which case I needn't ask the question I intended to ask. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And for the record, Your Honours, the exhibit number is 1D385.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Finally, Your Honours, I just forgot to tender the previous document concerning the measures of blockade. It is true that the witness said he was not familiar with the document; but he was familiar enough with the measures of blockade. He described what they consisted of and to whom they applied, and I believe this could be relevant. I therefore suggest that 1D00-0924 be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What does that add to the oral testimony of the witness though? I mean, the witness has described the events and measures that were in place, so what does the document add?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it adds the identification of who prescribed these measures, who adopted, who passed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D386, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Cross -- re-examination. Before Ms. Pidwell begins, for the record, the order admitting the last-mentioned document as an exhibit was by a majority; Judge Harhoff dissenting.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you were asked some questions by Mr. Krgovic, and I wanted to ask you just some clarifying questions now about those. You spoke about the meetings that you chaired in your role as the president of the SDS, and you said that there was never any talk about violence amongst -- against Muslims, about expelling them or any discrimination. Do you recall making that statement?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Now, I want to show you a document that -- that we looked at together.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: It's P ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: It was admitted -- sorry, under P377. Sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: It's P1619. Sorry, P1619.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Do you recall discussing this document, sir, which was the minutes of the Municipal Board meeting on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And you'll see --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: -- under the heading of Milan Kovacevic, that there was a discussion about the replacement of staff which had been carried out with all the SDA leaders removed from their functions in the Municipal Assembly. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Were any SDA leaders replaced under the direction of the Municipal Board?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not an order of the Municipal Board. This was done by the Crisis Staff after the takeover. The date is 9 May, so it was after the takeover and after the institution of the Crisis Staff. They did this. And as I said in my previous testimony, these are officials, officials. Those who held certain posts. Other employees remained in their places until the conflict broke out. I explained that even earlier, when you asked me the same thing. It's not in dispute. This was just discussed, in fact, reported, at the session of the Municipal Board.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Yes. But the -- the SDA leaders who took over, took over on the day of the takeover, didn't they? Not at this later date on the -- on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was just the inner circle, the main officials, the president of the Municipal Assembly, and a few other people whom I can't remember now. But these are just officials, not employees. And it says "officials" here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Yes, but were any Serb officials removed from their posts?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really remember. I think there were such cases too. Perhaps not immediately. Perhaps a bit later. If I can remember, Spiro Marmas [phoen], the recording secretary, I think he was also replaced. I think that happened too. But I can't give you any names. I wouldn't have been able to tell you about this either, if you hadn't shown me this document. In businesses, Serbs were replaced. One person was removed to make place for another. People resisted. That happened too. For instance, the director of the post office, Marko Pavic, who is now at the head of the municipality of Prijedor, he was removed as director, and Slavko - I can't remember the last name - was appointed in his stead. So, yes, people were replaced.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And the Serbs who you are talking about who were replaced, they were replaced with people who were submitting their names forward on behalf of the SDS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs. Yes. This was the core staff. But many people were replaced who were not even members of the SDS. For instance, the director of a large -- of a large enterprise. There was no general rule.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, let's have a look at another document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: P377, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, line 6, page 41, I don't think the witness's answer is properly recorded. As far as I understood, the witness said that many people were not replaced even if they were not members of the SDS. Perhaps Ms. Pidwell can --

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I appreciate if my friend wouldn't tell the witness what he thinks he heard, but rather just ask us to clarify that, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going ask the question again, and I'd ask to you repeat your answer, please. The Serbs who you were talking about being replaced, they were replaced with people whose names had been submitted on behalf of the SDS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were members of the SDS. They were members of the SDS. But I said there were also cases when executives were not members of the SDS but they were not members of the S [as interpreted], like director of Zitopromet, Vaso Cvijic. Marko Pavic, at the time, was not a member of the S; he was director of the post services. And he would later become member of the SDS in 1993, and he would occupy the highest post.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Let's have a look at P377, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, again, just the same. [Microphone not activated] ... the same mistake. This part is really missing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to not only speak clearly but to enunciate as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'm really in Your Honours' hands with this matter. I wonder whether we need to seek independent verification of what the witness has said, because it's twice that the Defence have intervened. And I'm not sure whether it's with -- the interpreters have not caught it or whether it's a different interpretation of what was said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, inasmuch as what the interpreters had last said, perhaps verification isn't going to assist. If -- if, in fact, the tapes are indistinct. So, Mr. Witness, you heard what the interpreters have indicated, that there is a problem in getting clearly what you are saying. So the -- Ms. Pidwell, I would ask you to try one more time. And, Mr. Witness, I would remind you of what the interpreters said, to speak into the microphone and speak as distinctly as possible so that there is no confusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, we were talking about people being replaced from their posts, and my question was: The Serbs who you said were being replaced in their posts were being replaced by people whose names were being submitted on behalf of the SDS. And can you try and please provide your answer for a third time, slowly.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those people were members of the SDS. They were nominated by the government, as reported by the president of the Executive Board, Mico Kovacevic, that is, the Crisis Staff. There were Serbs, executives, directors, who were replaced. Let's take the director of postal services, Marko Pavic, who is currently at the head of the municipality of Prijedor. He was then replaced by the -- as post office director by another man. There were cases when directors were not replaced, although they were members of the SDS -- although they were not members of the SDS. And I took as an example the director of Zitopromet, Vaso Cvijic, who remained the whole time in that post. Is it okay now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... third time, yeah. Finally, that's the correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And when you say Marko Pavic was replaced, was he replaced by another Serb or was he replaced by someone of another ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By a Serb, a member of the SDS. Later, in 1993, as I said, Marko would come to occupy a top post in the SDS party in Prijedor. But at that time, he wasn't a member.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Can we now have a look at document P377, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document dated the 28th of May. It's a dispatch, a telegram, to SJB chiefs from Stojan Zupljanin, stating that employees who did not sign the declaration shall be dismissed as of 15 April 1992. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see that. Perhaps the letters can be enlarged, although part of the text is very faint. All the employees who did not sign the solemn declaration --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have two objections: First, I don't see how this follows from my cross-examination; that's one objection. And then when you make a determination and after hearing from the Prosecutor, I can make the other objection. But there was no question in my cross-examination on this topic. And the witness, by the way, was not in the police at the time, so I don't see how he can answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That, too, occurred to me, Ms. Pidwell. How is this relevant in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I prefaced the -- this line of questioning, Your Honours, by taking you to the -- the portion in the transcript, 15277 onwards, where the witness talked about there being no discrimination against Muslims, no -- no -- no expulsions or measures taken or discussed in SDS meetings about these measures being taken. And he's -- so I took him to the first document which was when, in my submission, there was a discussion of a discriminatory nature. And then when he said that this only applied to the leadership, this document shows that it actually filtered down to employees and other members. And that's where I was going with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Let me hear Mr. Krgovic's second objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I didn't want to object to the line of questioning. My question about the meetings of the SDS was about the period before the takeover of power, and it -- the question was: At those meetings, before the takeover of power, was there talk of discriminatory measures? That was the line of my questioning. I was focussing narrowly on that topic. With no question of mine did I deal with the topic of the events after the takeover of power. You will not find that anywhere in my cross-examination. And, secondly, when the document was read to the witness, only part of the sentence was read to him, but not all of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, it seems to me that there is merit in Mr. Krgovic's objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, the -- the questions that were formulated by Mr. Krgovic from my recollection were not specific to the period before the takeover. If I can -- if you bear with me, Your Honours, I can take you to the appropriate portion in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, in any event, broadening this out, isn't it the -- a matter for inference and argument at the end of the day? How are the answers of this witness at this point going to assist?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, he has made some pretty broad statements about no discriminatory measures being put in place, and my questions were focussed on that, to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed, but within the confines of -- of -- the witness's knowledge of the -- if that's not stating the obvious. But I don't wish you to wonder too far afield.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Certainly, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, were you aware that police employees who did not sign the loyalty oath were dismissed from the new police force in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood your question to be, initially, as whether the SDS had on its agenda discriminatory measures toward other ethnicities, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... please answer the question --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to that I replied --

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Please answer the question that I've just put to you, which was --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: -- which was: Are you aware or were you aware that police employees were -- who did not sign the loyalty oath were dismissed?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
