utterances.text: Well, they are mostly policemen who I know. I met them even afterward. And, certainly, I got that information from them. And earlier, I wanted to explain, because you had also asked me about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move on to another topic now. You were questioned a number of times yesterday about the situation in Prijedor after the takeover, which occurred on the 30th of April. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And you described the situation in Prijedor as being calm until the 30th of May, when the Muslim forces attacked again. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Were you actually in Prijedor for the month of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And were you aware that the town of Hambarine was shelled in that month?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that was because two soldiers were killed in Hambarine. And since all measures and appeals to surrender the perpetrators of that attack were fruitless, the military dealt with the issue. So the police didn't have anything to do with it. And the military shot from their weapons. And the appeals were broadcast on Radio Prijedor, and many people insisted, called up the radio station on the phone, et cetera. Even Mirza Mujadzic called. I think it was before the takeover of power, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And, sir, are you also aware that the village of Brezevo was shelled in the month of May?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is neither Prezevo nor Brezevo in the municipality of Prijedor. There is no such place.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Maybe it's my pronunciation. Brizevo?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I don't remember any other occasion of shelling except for that one.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Well, you're familiar with the town of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And are you aware that the town of Kozarac was shelled?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I said as much, replying to a previous question of yours. I went even up to Dera to see some destroyed buildings and so on. But that's what I said earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Can we have a look at document, please. It's P00432/12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You are aware, of course, Ms. Pidwell, that this is a confidential document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have not shown this document to the witness, nor did I ask a line of questioning about this report, and I don't know how it can be useful to the Prosecution. The Prosecutor can ask the witness what she wants but not about this document, which I never showed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Perhaps we can go into private session while I deal with this issue, directing Your Honours about the reasons for the confidentiality and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That's also an answer to Mr. Krgovic's objection about relevance and whether this is something that arises out of cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour. The witness said on more than one occasion throughout the course of his cross-examination yesterday and today that the situation in Prijedor was calm until the Muslims attacked on the 30th of May. Now, it's the Prosecution's case -- and perhaps the witness can take off his headphones for this explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you [Microphone not activated] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: -- that the events in Prijedor in May were not calm. Indeed, a lot of villages were being shelled, mosques were being burned, people were being rounded up, the town of Kozarac was shelled and the inhabitants taken to Keraterm and Omarska. And so this document is a -- is a weekly bulletin of the police, stating that those events had taken place. I want to put it to him to see whether he wants to revise his testimony that the situation was, indeed, calm in the municipality at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, but this was a line of questioning pursued by the Prosecution in direct examination. The witness already replied to it in the direct examination. But in the cross-examination, I asked no questions about these events, neither about this report nor anything else. I only asked about Prijedor. I did not ask anything about Hambarine or Kozarac or any other settlement around Prijedor. I asked questions only about the town of Prijedor. The Prosecutor could have pursued this in the direct examination. If the Prosecutor is allowed to question the witness about this, then I seek permission to examine the witness again. The Prosecutor should have asked these questions in the examination-in-chief, rather than in the re-direct, because I never asked questions about these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to transcript page 15236 of the Prosecution examination-in-chief. That's where the Prosecution stopped and failed to ask any additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, these matters are covered by adjudicated facts. I did not in my examination-in-chief cover any items covered by adjudicated facts because we have the benefit of them and we have the limitation of time. When my learned friend Mr. Krgovic was cross-examining, on numerous occasions he asked the witness about the events in Prijedor and, particularly, after the takeover and relating to the attack by the Muslims. Now, the -- it was raised on no less than three occasions on -- during his cross-examination, and the upshot of that was that the witness was trying to say that after the events in Prijedor on the 30th of April, the situation was calm. There were no incidents. There was nothing happening. And he said that on numerous occasions under cross-examination. For example, page 1593 [sic] -- my learned friend asked the question: "... you didn't get a specific instruction on the 30th or" anything "around that date ..." "No, no." So this is 30th of April. "No, no. We just activated what existed on paper ..." And then he carries on to say: "There were no incidents, no conflicts, nothing. Like in any town, there were Muslim and Croat bars and other shops in Prijedor that were not touched. One can prove that. But later on, there was an escalation which had its consequences. But that's a different story." And what I'm trying to establish with Your Honours is that later on, being after the takeover, there was an escalation, and that conflicts did ensue in Prijedor. And that is what I'm trying to clarify in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Ms. Pidwell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, going back to the document, which is a confidential document, we may need to go into private session for my explanation on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And we're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, you have a document in front of you which is headed "Weekly Update" for the period of 8 to 25 May 1992. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And if we could turn, please, to the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you could enlarge it so I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And if can I direct you simply to -- it's an example to the first -- the third paragraph down: "On the territory covered by the centre, there were 23 explosions, 24 cases of law and order violations" and so forth. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And if we could turn to the next page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, before we leave this page, my eye just caught sight of the previous paragraph, which reads that: "The direct cause leading to the escalation of the situation in Prijedor area was an attack by the Muslim paramilitary units on a military vehicle and reservists returning home from the front line." My question to the witness is: Do you recall this incident, Mr. Miskovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I recall. It was dealt with in the examination-in-chief and in the cross-examination. It's the situation when the Muslim forces, the paramilitary units, attacked the soldiers belonging to the legal units returning home from the front line. And huge efforts were made to -- to find the perpetrators of that crime. An appeal was launched to the citizens to give information, and some citizens called the studio and commented on the event. That was explained. Both this case and the murder of the Serb police officer on -- on the road. I think that it was all clearly dealt with in Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Back to you, Ms. Pidwell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, let's just not spend too long on this document. But if we go to the top paragraph, if we're going backwards, you will see in the first paragraph it reads: "After an extended period of relative [sic] stable security situation in the area covered by the Banja Luka CSB, the past week brought fresh war destruction and new victims. The areas of Kupres, Bosanska Krupa call for additional effort on our part, and we are re-directing our forces to mopping up the area [sic] of Prijedor and Bihac." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Is that a reference to more police forces coming into the area of Prijedor because of unrest?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only assume as much. Because I see that this is a wider area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that there's a problem with the translation of the document. So if I could ask the interpreters to sight-translate this section.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Are the interpreters able to read the first paragraph of the document? If Your Honours require that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the first paragraph of what appears -- no, what appears is the first paragraph on this page of the English translation. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Our rules require that somebody in the courtroom read out the text and then we can interpret it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: All right. After --

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I think that requires someone to read out the Serbian text.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir -- if the witness could -- if you could read the first paragraph that you see in front of you.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could you read it out loud, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "After an extended period of a relatively calm security situation in the area of the Banja Luka CSB, the previous week brought about new war destruction and victims. The areas of Kupres and Bosanska Krupa still require additional efforts of ours, and we are re-directing our forces to improving the situation in the areas of Prijedor and Bihac. The situation is extremely complex ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was it, Your Honours, the difference between mopping up and improving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'll ask my question again then, sir. Is this, what you've just read out, on your understanding, a reference to more police forces coming into the area of Prijedor because of unrest?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what one can conclude, reading this paragraph, as help, or assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that the detention facilities of Omarska and Keraterm were established in the month of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact dates, when exactly it was. The Crisis Staff did that, and it was long ago. Even what I heard I -- I've forgotten till now. But Omarska, Keraterm - and what's the other called? - Trnopolje certainly existed. That's not in dispute. But when they were opened, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, in terms of the breaks, I always keep first and foremost in mind the rhythm which is necessary for those who have the care of the accused persons to be aware of, but bearing in mind that in fact our last 20-minute break was somewhat more than 60 seconds multiplied by 20, I'm wondering whether it would be practical for us to continue beyond the present time with a view to your completing your -- your re-examination. Or if you're going to be a substantial period of time, we may as well take the break to get back on track.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I think it's preferable to take the break now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, there's been a discussion over the break between counsel over scheduling for the balance of the week, and there is a -- one of the witnesses has a personal engagement which requires him to leave before -- before the weekend. And, accordingly, what the Prosecution is suggesting is that once we finish with this witness, we carry on to the next witness, ST-098, as scheduled. And we've spoken with the Defence counsel about the length of time for her -- for her cross-examination, which was -- probably won't exceed four hours in total, and then we are suggesting that we simply change the batting order of the subsequent witnesses so that we are -- we call, as the next witness, ST-163, in an effort to conclude his testimony and cross-examination before the weekend and then finalize with the two new witnesses. And, if necessary, one can spill over to the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are not going to discuss it before this witness. I think we should do so towards the end, because one has to take into account the Defence's ability to prepare for such changes. But we're not going to discuss it before the witness now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, during the course of your cross-examination, it was put to you that there were no armed clashes after the takeover on the 30th of April - and I'm referring specifically to page 15300 of the transcript - and you responded that there were none and that you, indeed, spoke to Mr. Cehajic after the conflict. And although he wasn't happy, you still had a discussion with him. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. But it wasn't after the conflict; it was after the takeover. It must have been a slip on your part.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And after the -- do you recall how long after the takeover you spoke with Mr. Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps the next day, or two, or maximum, three days later.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And do you know what happened to Mr. Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I didn't know. I found out later. I heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: When was the last time that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember exactly when I last saw him. I just told you when I spoke to him. His wife was a doctor, and I continued to see her for a while later, but I can't remember when exactly I saw him last. I -- I -- the last time we spoke, I can clearly see him in my mind's eye. He was in a white shirt without a tie. And I knew him because my brother taught in the high school together with him. My brother taught Serbian, and he taught history. My wife worked with his wife in the same hospital. My wife was a nurse, and his wife was a physician, a very nice lady.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: When you went to Omarska, did you ask about his whereabouts and why he was being detained there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not inquire about him or anyone else. I told you already, I didn't know who was detained there. I told you exactly how I came to be there, under what circumstances, and for how long. At that time, I didn't even know that he was there. I just supposed that many of those people knew me, although I was unable to recognise them at that time for the reasons that I already stated. I know that a large number of them knew me because of the work I did before the war, because of the post I held and later.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: So when did you actually find out that he was detained at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling, I don't know that he was detained in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked some questions by my learned friend - and I'm specifically referring to page 15287 of the transcript. You were asked some questions about the arming of the Muslim side. And you said, in answer to a question: "I said I didn't receive information directly, through my contacts. But I did hear it from military representatives that they are armed. Actually, both sides." And then, subsequently, Mr. Krgovic says: "... a correction to the transcript: When you said ... they had their structures and their weapons, you were referring to the Muslim and Croat side; right?" And you answered: "Yes, yes." I just want to clarify, sir, when you were talking about both sides, which sides were you talking about?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably the Muslims and Croats. I would like to hear the context of what I said. Perhaps it would make it easier.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Well, I can -- I've just read it out to you, sir, and you said "both sides." And Mr. Krgovic then said to you: "... you were referring to the Muslim and Croat side ..." in terms of being armed. And my question is: Who did mean when you said "both sides were being armed"?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most probably the Muslims and Croats, because the Serbs in the army and the police, were armed. Because they were under military command. Some under army command, others under police command, and they had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that the military representatives told you that the Muslims and Croats were armed and then you said: "Actually, both sides." Are you referring to the Muslims and Croats being armed on the one hand or the Serbs being armed on the on the other hand, or are you just referring to the Muslims and Croats being armed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It's not cross-examination, Your Honour. Asked an answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, I confess I too had some difficulty with that question. I heard it, but I was trying to process it before Mr. ... and I suppose my reservation was not dissimilar to Mr. Krgovic's formal objection. You are, of course, re-examining.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, and I'm simply wanting to clarify the transcript at the moment. At the moment, the transcript says one thing as the witness's answer, and then a leading question is put by my learned friend correcting that and suggesting that the two sides that were being referred to were the Muslim and Croats. And I'm wanting to establish with the witness whether, indeed, he meant that the Muslims and Croats were being amend; or did he mean the two sides, being the Muslims and Croats on the one hand, and the Serbs on the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, he's heard the question. If he is able to answer, he may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, when you're talking about both sides being armed in this context, are you talking about the Muslims and the Croats on the one hand, and the Serbs on the other; or are you referring solely to the Muslims and the Croats on --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Objection. It's leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Pidwell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll repeat.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, when you're talking about two sides -- I'll read your answer to you. Well, I'll read the question; that may help you further. The question was: "As far as I understood you, you didn't hear from the Muslim side that they have all that, but you got ... information that [sic] the army, that there were such plans and such units and so on?" And you said: "I said that I didn't receive information directly, through my contacts. But I did hear it from military representatives that they are armed. Actually, both sides."

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Armies.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: When you say the words "both sides," which side do you mean on the one hand and which side do you mean on the other hand?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Croat and the Muslim sides, because the Serb side was armed through military units, where they were involved, and police units, where they were involved. We already spoke about that in great detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, you were further asked some questions today, earlier today, about the town of Kozarac, and you answered that basically the events that took place in Kozarac were done by the army and that -- but that you said it was your idea, "our idea," and that nobody from the region was involved in the negotiations with Kozarac. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the talks and negotiations are concerned, the talks to prevent the conflict, we had a large number of talks and numberless contacts when we met officially and unofficially and it was all geared toward the same end. However, we did not make the decision to attack Kozarac. That was done by the army. And as you saw a moment ago, they had information about arming and the level of weapons, and they decided on operations to be launched in Hambarine, in Kozarac, and in other places where it was needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: You were asked specifically whether Mr. Zupljanin took part in the talks about Kozarac. Did Simo Drljaca take part in the talks or the negotiations that were about Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Kozarac and other areas are concerned, Drljaca was involved, Stakic, myself, Mico Kovacevic. We were all involved in these talks. I think we've already discussed this. There is also the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, you were also asked some questions about the conditions at Omarska camp. And you said, in response to a report that was shown to you, that you had some involvement with a building at Omarska and that it had been made for "that purpose." I think it's recorded at page 16 today. What -- what purpose are you referring to? What was the purpose of the -- of this Omarska structure before it became a camp in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to be section commander, that is, in the police in Omarska, and from that level I had direct contacts with the leadership of the Ljubija mine, which commandeered land for the needs of the mine. And Hidrogradnja, Sarajevo. I think Pozder [phoen] was the name of the project manager. And in that context I was familiar with the work and the building done there. Buildings for administration were being built, and a big refectory, cafeteria, something like a factory, restaurant, where workers could go, wash their hands. That's the information I had until then, until that visit. And I used to work there as police section commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Were you aware of any bedrooms or dormitories or anything of that nature at Omarska, in that building?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I did not. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: When you went there, did you see where the detainees slept?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. I told you, I just saw the outside. And I told you they were standing outside. And as I was going up the stairs, I saw them only the time it took me to pass by and go upstairs. I don't know any of these buildings, the -- the administrative buildings or the halls.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And you recall you were asked some questions about -- and shown a photograph about -- there was some confusion over which building you actually went into. You weren't sure whether it was the building you marked number 1 or number 3. Are you able to recall, when you entered the building with this delegation, whether there was cafeteria there or not?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. I can't remember. I hear it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: So you don't recall seeing people eating, a cafeteria, a restaurant-type facility, when you walked in with this delegation?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I really don't recall. Most probably we were given a snack or a drink, juice or coffee. They must have served something. I -- I still don't know whether it's the -- it was from a cafeteria or from a makeshift facility. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: You were also asked some questions about Mr. Krajisnik being involved in -- in -- with the continuation of Simo Drljaca's role. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that. Not the role, but the replacement of Simo Drljaca as chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Are you aware that he went on to become the assistant minister of the interior in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simo Drljaca? No. The first time I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: So who took over from his role as the SJB chief in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dusan Jankovic, professional policeman. He used to be commander of the traffic police in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And when did he take over?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Simo was replaced.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Are you able to assist us with -- a little bit more with the date?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't. All I know it was after that session, the standing session of the Municipal Assembly, regarding the replacement of executive staff in the municipality. I don't even know when that session took place. It was, in fact, a session of the municipality, the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: If we can have a look at a document, please. It's P759.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Have a look at this, sir. It may assist you in remembering the date, or providing some context to it. It's a publication dated the 9th of April, 1993, and it's an interview with Simo Drljaca. And it's headed: "Interview with Simo Drljaca, assistant minister of the interior of the Republika Srpska Krajina, with regard to his role in the chief affair."

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sorry, if we could, on the B/C/S, to -- just make it a little bit smaller so we see the heading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see it. It's too small.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: May I inquire, Ms. Pidwell, why is it that you're in, re-examination, pursuing this collateral issue with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Well, sir, the witness gave evidence in cross-examination that the SDS did not stand behind Simo Drljaca and that -- and testified about him being removed, and I'm trying to establish when that happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. But we have the document in evidence. It's -- isn't the rest of it left for arguments at the end of the day, if this is an issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Well, if Your Honour is happy with that, I will -- I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, I now want to direct your attention to a couple of questions asked by Mr. Cvijetic earlier today. And, in particular, I'm referring to page 26 and 27 of the transcript, and Mr. Cvijetic was talking to you about Variant B. And I just wanted to clarify. Mr. Cvijetic said: "The way I understood Variant B ... in essence, was the establishment of Serb authorities and Serb municipalities in an area where the Serbs were the majority population."

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Except I added to that and I explained: In parts of the municipality where Serbs were a majority. If you remember, that was my explanation, because I stopped halfway to explain how the witness -- how I understood the witness explained it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I just want to clarify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, did Variant B apply to municipalities where there was a Serb majority or a Serb minority?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minority. The Serbs were in a minority in such areas where representatives of other ethnic communities held power.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And further on, you talked about the presence of the White Eagles in Prijedor. Who were the White Eagles?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three men who had proclaimed themselves to be White Eagles, they were immediately detained by the army, interrogated, and I believe a criminal complaint was filed against them. It's the only incident that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honours, I'm sorry, I have to interject. Mr. Cvijetic was making signals to the witness. He cleared his throat, he tapped on the side of the desk with his hand. That's not the first time he's done it. And I have to bring it to your attention because it's highly improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I confess I didn't observe it, Mr. Hannis. And if Mr. Hannis's observation is correct, then, Mr. Cvijetic, you would desist.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will not do it anymore. I was just stopping the witness from speaking so fast. He keeps rushing in his speech. We have enormous problems with the transcript as it is. I was trying to prevent him from going on at that rate. And I won't do it anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think Mr. Hannis is the last person who should teach an attorney-at-law how to conduct himself in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, gentlemen, now that we understand what this is about, we will -- let's get back on track. Ms. Pidwell, please continue. Mr. Hannis, do you need to pursue this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have to respond to Mr. Krgovic's remark, Your Honour. I think I have an obligation, as counsel in court, to try and ensure the integrity of the proceedings. I reported something I saw not for the first time. If that's what he's trying to do, which is legitimate exercise, the appropriate way to do is to address it with you. Not directly with the witness who's sitting nearly in his lap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Cvijetic's explanation is that he now appreciates that his efforts to be helpful may have been misinterpreted. And he has agreed to conform his behaviour in the future to dealing with matters like this in a manner that would not invite controversy. So the matter is settled, and we can move on. Yes, Ms. Pidwell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I just need to get back to where -- where we were.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, you -- we were talking about the White Eagles and their presence in Prijedor, and you've explained who they are. Are you able to explain when they arrived in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't arrive. Three people from Prijedor suddenly became self-proclaimed White Eagles. But they were immediately apprehended by the military police and detained. And I believe that they were tried. I just want to show, with that, that there were some individuals who tried to do some things, but they were neutralized immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And just finally, sir, you were asked some questions about a document, referring to people needing permission to leave the municipality, and you -- you said that even you needed a document in order to -- to leave the municipality at this time. From whom would you obtain that -- that documentation?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the Crisis Staff. For going to Serbia, as far as I remember, I had to take out a permit from the -- from the draft office so -- confirming that I was not a deserter or something like. I do know that my brother-in-law, my wife's brother, died in Kosovska Mitrovica. We wanted to go there, to the funeral, but we weren't allowed to cross the border. So she couldn't attend the funeral.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. I have a comment on the -- on the transcript. Could the witness just repeat from whom he needed a permission to go to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, I needed a certificate from the People's Defence to show that you were travelling officially or that you weren't in -- a deserter. But as far as, I said it was from the People's Defence that you had to get it. Because some sort of guarantee was required that the person questioned would not desert or run away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, you have explained to us during your testimony in the last couple of days how the situation became very tense in Prijedor and how much fear was felt by most of the inhabitants in Prijedor and surrounding villages. You explained to us that on the 25th of April there was a meeting that took place in Cirkin Polje and that another meeting was then held on the 29th of April, four days later, to discuss these issues. And you told us that, at the last occasion, it was decided to actually take over control in Prijedor, and you told us that this was decided in order to retain the relative calmness and peace that still existed. So you told us that the purpose of the takeover was to keep things under control. Now, please, Mr. Miskovic, wait and listen to my questions. I have two questions to you. The first question is whether, to your knowledge, the CSB in Banja Luka was informed about the discussions to take over control in Prijedor and, ultimately, whether the CSB in Banja Luka was informed when the decision was made on the 29th of April to take over control in Prijedor. Do you know if -- if the -- if the actors who were involved in the discussions and the decision to take over control in Prijedor, were they in constant communication and contact with the CSB in Banja Luka; do you know that? That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I explained in detail that after that dispatch, we spoke about that. But I arrived when the decision was already made. The structure about which I spoke had already been in place. And I arrived when there was only talk about what should be done and when. And the meeting was called for 2.00 a.m., and the representatives of the TO, Mr. Kuruzovic, and the police representative, Mr. Drljaca, briefed everybody present about the situation. And then the implementation began at 4.00 a.m. Whether they had any previous commands [as interpreted] with the command of the corps or with the CSB, I don't know because I wasn't informed of it. And according to the dispatch we analysed here, Simo did submit a report to the CSB later that there had been a takeover of power. But nobody informed me. I wasn't up-to-date whether there was information flow toward the military or police structures. The garrison commander, Colonel Arsic, and his deputy, the TO commander, the representatives of the police, and so on, were there, and I came there after a meeting at the MUP. They were already sitting there and taking decisions. I have already explained as much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. My question was prompted by the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I have a slight correction of the transcript. The witness, on page 69, line 21 -- "whether they had any previous commands" is what the transcript reads, but the witness said "contact," rather than "commands."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krgovic. I understood as much. But just to round up to you, Mr. Miskovic. My question was prompted by the information you gave or that we have seen in the documents that were shown to you, that apparently about 1500 policemen were involved in the action, so my question to you was whether you had any information that the CSB in Banja Luka had been advised about where things were going in -- in Prijedor. My second question to you goes to the -- the purpose of this action, really. Because you told us that the decision to take over control in Prijedor was prompted by the attempt to keep things under control and prevent escalation of a conflict that was already brewing, and so you decided to take over control of the town by assuming power of the Municipal Assembly, and the SJB, and all the public institutions that could you get your hands on. And we also saw the evidence by Mr. Kovacevic that, subsequent to this, the -- the leading SDA members in the Municipal Assembly were dismissed and replaced by Serbs. Now, my question to you is: Did you, at the time, think that this would prevent the conflict from escalating? Did you really believe that this would keep things under control? To be honest, my immediate reaction would have been the opposite; that, if any of the parties involved in negotiation certainly decide unilaterally to take power, that would almost inevitably prompt a counter-response from the other parties involved in the negotiations, so that by taking over power, you may perhaps have achieved a few days, or maybe a week of silence, but soon thereafter, you were bound to have reactions from the Muslim and the Croat societies, and, indeed, you did get reactions. So I'm curious to know, from someone who was involved in the events at the time, what was really the wisdom of this? Was there a major plan behind it? Or how could you possibly have thought that this would calm down things? Can you answer me?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. I'm glad you asked me this question, although we've spoken about that in the examination. It is true, as you put it, that until that time there was peace. But the basic reason for taking over control, as has been confirmed several times over, was not the immense desire to rule or dominate somebody; but, on the contrary, to prevent confrontation. Control wasn't taken over, nor was any activity to that effect taken, and no Serb municipality was established from local communes in the Prijedor municipality until this dispatch arrived, which required the Croatian and Muslim forces, that is, citizens, to intercept military vehicles, attack barracks, block roads. It has been read here. I don't have to enumerate it all. That was the fuse that set it all off. And the only possibility was to take over control, when that dispatch arrived to prevent the people from attacks barracks and so on, and I had the opportunity -- or, rather, everybody in Prijedor had -- had had the opportunity to see what happened in Croatia before that, and in Slovenia, with attacks barracks and so on. In order to prevent all that, the decision was taken to take over control. It was only for these reasons that this was done. And it can be seen from the documents that there haven't been any incidents in that context until the attack on those soldiers that were coming from back from the front line at Hambarine. And that triggered the reaction of the army. After the agreement that the military would secure the road to Banja Luka, there was a roadblock set up in Kozarac. And those were the reasons for taking over control. It wasn't anybody's desire to dominate. But we have already seen that in the examination of the OTP and the Defence. And the genesis of it all has also been explained. It isn't all black and white. In the Balkans and in former Yugoslavia, the memories of such events go back a long time. If you have additional questions or if you're not satisfied with my answer, go ahead and ask me some more questions. I'll be glad to answer, if I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Miskovic. You have indeed answered my questions. And I realize that the scramble for power is something that goes a long way back in your history. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Miskovic. We are grateful for your assistance to the Tribunal. Your testimony is at an end, and you're now released. We wish that you have a safe journey back to your home. The usher would now escort you from the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too. And I'm glad if I could make a modest contribution to establishing the truth about the events in Prijedor municipality. Thank you once more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before the next witness is called, we have a brief oral ruling which is as follows: The Trial Chamber is seized of the oral request made by the Defence on the 30th of September and the 4th of October to postpone the testimony of the witness Ewan Brown, the Prosecution's military expert, to the end of the Prosecution's case, or, alternatively, to postpone his cross-examination. The Prosecution responded on both occasions. The Trial Chamber notes that it is in the interests of justice that the Defence be in a position to prepare fully for the cross-examination of Ewan Brown. Given that he is scheduled to commence testifying on the 20th of October and the extensive material, including the Mladic material, some of which was only disclosed in mid-September, that the Defence will need to review to cross-examine Ewan Brown effectively, the Trial Chamber will only hear his examination-in-chief in October, and considering the witness's busy schedule, he shall appear for again for cross-examination during the week commencing the 10th of January, 2011. Thank you. Yes, is the Prosecution ready with its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to take advantage of the time before the witness is called to discuss the schedule for this week. I believe that Ms. Pidwell, citing the conversation with the Defence, misinterpreted our agreement. Ms. Korner left the courtroom with the latest information that she related to the us, that Witness ST-163 most probably would be postponed for next week because of private commitments. And also, with regard to the pace of the proceedings this week, we see no other solution but this, and this what I believe was our informal agreement. If there should be a reshuffling witness, that is, if Witness ST-163 could be heard immediately after the expert witness, Ms. Tabeau, we believe that it would be detrimental to the Defence because in this situation we are unable to keep up with this rapid pace and the ambitious list of the OTP for this week. The witness who has testified already is relevant, and so his examination took quite some time. We also expect Ms. Tabeau's testimony to be relevant. And the same applying to ST-163. All three of these witnesses have the support of extensive documentation and materials, which makes us unable to efficiently prepare for such a sudden change of -- in the order of appearance of the witnesses. This is detrimental to the interests of the Defence, and we will not be able to accommodate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, we are not quite certain of the immediate schedule. Is the plan to hear Mrs. Tabeau now, and then move on straight from her to Witness 163? Is that the plan? Or do you request to have 163 brought to the stand immediately now?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, you're right that we propose to call Ms. Tabeau now. And -- and then -- the only change is to move the crime-based witness up to after ST-163 who has a family commitment on Saturday to ensure that can actually return home for that. And we have made some inquires with the Registry to see if -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I understand --

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: -- so it's just that small reshuffle. And in my submission, Your Honours, if the Defence are unable to keep up with the speed of the trial this week, it's their choice to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pidwell. Mr. Cvijetic, it seems that we will now hear the expert witness, Ms. Tabeau, today, and probably most of tomorrow. Then for Thursday, we will hear Witness 163. And that's according to the schedule. So you're not losing out on any time, as far as I can see. According to the schedule that we have in front of us, Witness 163 is scheduled for Thursday and Friday of this week. So what is your problem exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you didn't mention that Witness 227 was supposed to testify before him. ST-227. And the Prosecution applied for two and a half hours for him, and the Defence also applied for as much time. That is at least one more day. And bearing in mind the time allotted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Cvijetic, if I understood Ms. Pidwell correct, the plan is simply to skip Witness 227 at this point and hear him at a later stage. So we will move straight from the expert, Dr. Tabeau, to Witness 163. He was scheduled to arrive here and begin his testimony on Thursday, the 7th of October, and that is, indeed, what he will do. So you cannot, with any strength, claim that you haven't had time to prepare his -- his testimony -- to prepare for his testimony, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when we get the schedule, we prepare accordingly. Now, suddenly, we have to prepare for ST-163 because ST-227 has been skipped. This disturbs our preparation process for the cross-examination. That is the problem. Because we proceed according to schedule. And now this change has come very suddenly. We have too little time to prepare for Witness 163.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, we see no merit in your objection, and it's -- it's on the record, but we over -- we see no reason why the Prosecution cannot proceed in the -- ought not to proceed in the manner in which they proposed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, my colleague, Mr. Di Fazio, will be leading the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before that, if I may, I would like to raise a procedural matter. Today is a deadline for us to reply to the Prosecution's submission about the calling of a witness about adjudicated facts. In the previous trials where they were testified, they were accorded protective measures, so I would like to seize the opportunity to raise this matter orally so that we needn't respond in writing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I would object to that. The Defence were directed to file a response by today. The deadline for that is 4.00 this afternoon, or 12.00 midnight. And we have a witness waiting outside. I would -- the normal course of action is for Defence to reply in writing to written motions, rather than use valuable court time to deal with something while we've got a witness outside. And we're on a tight schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just wanted to utter a single sentence. But if that's a waste of time, okay, we can put it on paper. I just wanted to be more efficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what's the single sentence, Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We take no position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, madam. I trust you can hear us in a language you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you for coming down and give us your testimony in this trial. May I start out by asking you to read the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, madam. You may be seated. Madam, would you be good enough to tell us your name and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Ewa Tabeau. I was born on 26th of April, 1958.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm a demographer. I'm the chief of Demographic Unit in the ICTY Prosecutor's Office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Tabeau, you are aware of the fact that you have been called here in this trial against Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin, who are sitting here, as an expert in respect of the demographic changes that took place during the time that is covered by this indictment. We have carefully studied your reports, and they have been admitted into evidence. The Prosecution -- or maybe I should ask you first, but I thought it was redundant because it appears from your reports that you have, indeed, testified earlier, but can you tell us in which cases you have testified -- in the -- in the capacity of an expert?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I testified so far 14 times in the -- as an expert witness for the Prosecutor -- Prosecution. And one time I was called by the Defence. I was an expert for the Defence. I testified in cases such as Slobodan Milosevic. I testified in Sarajevo cases, that would be Dragomir Milosevic and General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Galic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- Galic. Yes, sir. I testified in Popovic, that would be Srebrenica. I testified in Lukic and Lukic. I testified in Simic et al. I testified in the Stakic case, in Prijedor. I might have missed some, but the list of my testimonies, I believe, is attached with my qualifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you ever testified as an expert in relation to the events which you have covered in your expert reports before other courts than this court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let me get back to the plan that I was going to line out for you, then. The Prosecution, represented by Mr. Di Fazio, has requested two hours to examine you in-chief on the basis of the reports that have been admitted into evidence. And each of the two teams for Defence have requested four hours, each of them. And as I know that you are well familiar with the procedures here, I need not tell you that you are required to give truthful answers and that there is a severe penalty for providing false or incomplete evidence or information to the Chamber, and finally that your quality as expert witness makes it possible for you to offer evaluations rather than just mere facts that pertain to the case. This is as much as I would have to say at this stance, so I give the floor to Mr. Di Fazio to go through the CV with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps before I do that, if I could just continue in the vein that Your Honour has just set out, namely, some introductory matters, part of which have been addressed by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You're here today and tomorrow to basically testify about three -- three reports. Firstly is a report that you prepared back in 2003, entitled the -- or titled: "The Ethnic Composition: Internally Displaced Persons and Refugees from 47 municipalities for 1991 to 1997/1998," and that's the -- I'm going to refer to that as Milosevic report. That's one of your reports, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: For the record, that's 65 ter 10.398.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The second report, principle report, that you're going to tell us about and discuss is an addendum to that report that you prepared specifically for this case. And, again, that deals with ethnic composition and internally displaced persons, and that was prepared in April of last year but is more confined and only deals with the indictment municipalities in this case. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: For the record that is 10399, 65 ter 10399.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The third report that you're going to -- sorry, perhaps before I go on to the third report, there's one other matter I should raise in relation to this addendum report, and that is: Before the summer break, you had occasion to -- to review that particular report, the addendum report prepared specifically for this case, and you had to make some corrections, and you prepared a -- an addendum. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Not to the report on IDPs and refugees. I did prepare an addendum, but it was to the third report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. My apologies. You're quite right. You had to replace some pages from -- from the -- from the addendum report, and -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: In the IDPs report, in detail, I think three pages were replaced. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And if Your Honours please, those replacement pages in the record is 65 ter 10399.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And the third major report that you will discuss is the one entitled "Victims of War," related to the Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin indictment. That's dated February of this year. And is -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. It was the third report, victims report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, that's 65 ter 10400.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You also then create -- added an addendum or correction to that report, and that was the one that you -- you prepared just before the summer break, and that consists of about three pages. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And if Your Honours please, that's 65 ter 10400.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In addition, given the size of your reports, you've prepared two summaries from two of those reports. The summary of results dealing with ethnic composition and internally displaced persons, derived from the report on displacement of persons prepared specifically for this case.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And if Your Honours please, that's 65 ter 10397.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And finally, a summary that you prepared from your third and final report, the "Victims of War" report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And if Your Honours please, that's 65 ter 10400.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The -- go through the nature and objective of each report. The Milosevic report, I believe, is quite wide. It covers 47 municipalities and also includes the 18 municipalities that you focussed on for your second report specific to this case?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It mostly covers what is the present-day Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. That is generally the truth. There were some areas in the Federation, but in majority is the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. In that report, you set out the -- the methodology adopted by you in writing these reports concerning population displacement in the sections dealing with objective and scope at pages 4 to 10 of that report, and Annex C, at pages 226 to 231 of that report.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That's correct. In addition to this, in Annex B, sources used for this report were discussed in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Thank you. Essentially, the objective of the Milosevic report was to provide a report on the ethnic composition in Bosnia and the minimum numbers of internally displaced persons and refugees in Bosnia. And, of course, when I say "Bosnia," I'm talking about the 47 municipalities that were the subject of that study.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. It is correct. It is also not wrong to say in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as the Milosevic, the 47 municipalities, were a subset of the analyses completed for all municipalities in the entire country. Regarding the ethnic composition, we looked at the change in ethnic composition at the outbreak of the war and after the war, in 1991 and -- versus later, 1997/1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now the addendum report that you prepared for this case, specifically for this case, is, as I said earlier, essentially the same as the Milosevic report but limited in scope to 18 municipalities?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: However, you used the same analyses, the same statistical sources, and there was the same objective in the report, except that it was more confined, less municipalities?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is all correct. As the methodology and sources were used for the entire country, the entirety Bosnia-Herzegovina. So the subset of 18 is just part of the overall area of the entire country.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. And the third report that you've -- third principle report that you've mentioned, the "Victims of War" report, you correct me if I'm wrong, but that is essentially a report dealing with the numbers of deaths arising from the war in the period 1st of April, 1992, to 31st of December, 1992, and covering the indictment area?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. And this is the number of deaths, war-related deaths on the first place, but also missing persons. Missing persons are part of that analysis as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And this report covers the war-related deaths of both soldiers and civilians?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The methodology, I believe, is contained in section 2.1 at pages 2 to 4?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. And there is another related paper which explains the methodology and sources, the so-called "Berlin paper," conference paper, which is associated in some way with this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I dislike stopping you at this -- abruptly at this point, but I'm advised that you need a minute -- the OTP needs a minute, before we take the adjournment in 30 seconds, to deal with a housekeeping matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I've got one more question, and that will wrap up this particular topic. I'll then -- tomorrow, I can move on to her other issues of expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And finally, the last question for today: On this "Victims of War" report, unlike the other two, the Milosevic report and the addendum report prepared specifically for this case, the "Victims of War" report is based on 12 databases of statistics and numbers that you obtained from Bosnia; essentially is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Essentially, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, this would be a convenient time, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, we are -- you're well-versed in the court schedules, and we're about to take the break for today to resume in this chamber at 9.00 tomorrow morning. The -- we have a brief housekeeping matter which we will deal with as the usher escorts you from the courtroom. Thank you, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have two. The first one regards scheduling this week. Out of an abundance of caution, the Prosecution would like to request the possibility of an extended sitting on Thursday afternoon in order that we can complete all the witnesses scheduled for this week. I understand that there may be a courtroom available. And if Your Honours are willing to consider that, I wanted to make the request now so we can plan accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Registry confirms that there would be a courtroom available.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. The second matter concerns --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry. One session, or ... when you say "extended sitting," one further session or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not sure. I think we'll have a better feel for that when we see how quickly we go with Ms. Tabeau. I would ask for two sessions now out of an abundance of caution and then adjust accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: From the Chamber's point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: From the Chamber's point of view, it looks as if we may be able to accommodate one session on Thursday. We would see what the -- inquire as to the Defence convenience, and they can respond first thing tomorrow morning. You said there was a second matter, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The second regarded the witness Ewan Brown. I think, when Ms. Pidwell advised you earlier in the week about his situation in our efforts to try and have him done during that week of October 20th to the 22nd, now in light of Your Honours' decision, Ms. Korner has asked me to advise the Court that it would be the Prosecution's intention to try and present his entire evidence in the new year, rather than have a bifurcation between his testimony in direct and cross-exam. And the reason for that is his professional schedule. I don't know the exact details, but I do recall he has some sort of 90-day contract of work he's doing in a place far away, and he was able to give us five days in October. But I don't know that he can give us five days in October and five or seven days in January. So it's the Prosecution's intention, and we would then schedule somebody else for three days in October now. I just wanted to notify everyone that that's our intention. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So we take the adjournment to tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 6th day of October, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.49 p.m.,
